name: docker-client
//version: The product's single source of truth for the running version: the client reads it at build time (client/app-version.ts) and displays it in the About notice. The client and server workspaces stay at 0.0.0 on purpose — see their own note.
author: Christian Mariani
//start: The single command that builds and serves the whole application on one port. The order and the && are load-bearing, not tidiness: build runs the client before the server because the server process serves the client's output from client/dist, and a failed link stops the chain, so a broken build never leaves the previous build running as if the command had worked. serve runs the built server and rebuilds nothing, so a restart costs no build time. dev:client and dev:server are the separate two-process development flow and are no part of this chain.

scripts.start: npm run build && npm run serve
scripts.build: npm run build -w client && npm run build -w server
scripts.lint: npm run lint:swarm-absence && npm run lint:clean-daemon && npm run lint -w client
scripts.//lint:clean-daemon: The second check that spans both test trees, so it lives here too: every daemon-backed test file starts from a daemon it emptied itself. The two trees are wired differently — a per-file call in the end-to-end specs, a preload for the server pass — so the guard reads both.
scripts.//lint:swarm-absence: The one check that spans both source trees, so it lives here rather than in a workspace: swarm left the product on 2026-08-27 and this is what keeps it gone. It is also the whole automated proof that a daemon in swarm mode changes nothing, no check of this project ever initialising a swarm.
scripts.test: npm run lint:swarm-absence && npm run lint:clean-daemon && npm run test -w server && npm run test -w client
scripts.//test:e2e:per-file: One file at a time, each with its own timestamps, so a slow spec can be told from a slow suite. Two details it cannot do without. The path is passed relative to the client workspace (`e2e/name.spec.ts`), which is what Playwright matches against. And **a failing file's traces are copied out of the repository before the next file starts** — Playwright empties `client/test-results/` at the start of every run, so a trace left there is a trace the next file destroys; the first version of this script lost one that way. A failing file does not stop the loop: its exit code is printed and the next file starts, since the point is to time all of them.
scripts.test:e2e:per-file: for f in $(ls client/e2e/*.spec.ts); do t=${f#client/}; echo ""; echo "=== $t"; s=$(date +%s); echo "start $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')"; npm run test:e2e -w client -- --quiet "$t"; r=$?; e=$(date +%s); if [ $r -ne 0 ]; then d="$HOME/Desktop/vexel-traces-$(date '+%Y-%m-%d')/${t##*/}"; mkdir -p "$d"; cp -R client/test-results/. "$d"/ 2>/dev/null; echo "traces kept in $d"; fi; echo "end   $(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')  took $((e-s))s  exit $r"; done
